Once dominated by Sunni insurgents, Anbar has been the scene of many attacks on U.S.-led troops in Iraq. Now a bastion of tribal opposition, it is also the scene of an internal Sunni political struggle between the Iraqi Islamic Party, one of Iraq's main Sunni parties, and the Awakening movement, the first anti-al Qaeda in Iraq movement established in the country. More than 25,000 U.S. troops serve in the sprawling Anbar province west of Baghdad; most of them Marines. They will remain for the time being but will shift their mission to supporting Iraqi forces, when needed . The transfer is a "major progress" for all of Iraq, said Brigadier Gen. Anbar is the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to revert to local security control, but is the first Sunni-dominated one. # Coalition Forces Transfer Security Control of Anbar Province to Iraqi Authorities

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) — Coalition forces formally transferred security control of Iraq's Anbar province to Iraqi authorities on Monday, marking a significant milestone in a region that once served as the epicenter of the country's Sunni insurgency.

President George W. Bush hailed the handover as a decisive victory against al-Qaeda extremists who had previously exerted considerable influence in the area. "Today, Anbar is no longer lost to al Qaeda—it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar," he stated.

Once a stronghold of Sunni insurgent activity and the site of numerous attacks against U.S.-led forces, Anbar has since transformed into a center of tribal resistance against extremism. The province now finds itself at the heart of an internal Sunni political rivalry, pitting the Iraqi Islamic Party—one of Iraq's principal Sunni political factions—against the Awakening movement, the pioneering anti-al-Qaeda coalition established within the country.

More than 25,000 U.S. troops, predominantly Marines, are stationed throughout the expansive province west of Baghdad. While these forces will remain in the region for the foreseeable future, their role will transition to providing support for Iraqi security forces as needed.

Brigadier General David Perkins, spokesman for the Multi-National Force in Iraq, characterized the handover as "major progress" for the nation as a whole. The transfer ceremony was held in Ramadi, the provincial capital, and drew attendance from Iraqi officials and senior U.S. military leadership.

"We are all well aware of what the security situation was in Anbar even a year ago," Perkins remarked. "And the fact that that has been able to be turned around, that the Iraqi citizens that live there want to stand up on their own, that they want to take control of the province on their own... it's a major progress not only for Anbar, but for all of Iraq."

With this transfer, Anbar becomes the eleventh of Iraq's eighteen provinces to assume local security control—and notably, the first Sunni-majority province to do so. This development coincides with a substantial decline in violence across Iraq and growing pressure from Iraqi leaders urging the United States to establish a concrete timetable for troop withdrawal.

The provinces that have previously transitioned to Iraqi security control include Duhuk, Irbil, and Sulaimaniya in the Kurdish region, along with Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra, and Maysan in southern, Shiite-majority Iraq.

*CNN's Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon contributed to this report from Baghdad.*

These forces will maintain their positions for now, though their role will transition toward providing backup support to Iraqi security personnel as circumstances require.

The formal ceremony marking this transition occurred in Ramadi, the provincial capital, with both Iraqi government representatives and senior American military officials in attendance.

This development coincides with a substantial decline in overall violence throughout Iraq, alongside mounting pressure from Iraqi citizens demanding that American officials establish a concrete schedule for withdrawing troops.

Previously transferred provinces include the Kurdish territories of Duhuk, Irbil, and Sulaimaniya, plus several Shiite-majority regions in the south: Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra, and Maysan.

CNN correspondents Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon contributed additional reporting from Baghdad for this article.

# Coalition Forces Hand Over Security Control of Anbar Province to Iraqi Authorities

In a significant development in Iraq's ongoing security transition, coalition troops formally transferred security control of Anbar province to Iraqi forces on Monday. The handover represents a major milestone in the broader effort to shift responsibility for the country's stability from foreign military forces to Iraqi institutions.

President George W. Bush hailed the transfer as a substantial victory in the fight against al-Qaeda, framing the development in terms that underscored a fundamental shift in the province's dynamics. Rather than characterizing the situation as al-Qaeda losing its grip due to external pressure alone, Bush emphasized that the terrorist organization had effectively lost control of Anbar, highlighting a change driven significantly by local rejection of extremist elements within the province itself.

This transition marks a striking transformation for a region that was once synonymous with the Sunni insurgency and served as the staging ground for numerous deadly attacks against coalition forces. For years, Anbar was considered one of the most dangerous and volatile areas in Iraq, presenting significant challenges to American and allied military operations. The province's evolution from a insurgent stronghold to a candidate for local security control illustrates the complex and often unpredictable nature of Iraq's security landscape.

However, the handover comes amid new challenges, as Anbar now finds itself embroiled in internal political tensions. A power struggle has emerged between the Iraqi Islamic Party and the Awakening movement, two influential groups vying for political dominance in the post-insurgency landscape. This internal friction underscores that while security concerns tied to insurgent violence may have diminished, the province still faces significant governance and political challenges as various factions seek to establish their influence.

Despite the formal transfer of security responsibilities, the American military presence in Anbar will remain substantial. More than 25,000 U.S. troops, the majority of them Marines, will continue to operate in the province, providing support to Iraqi forces as they assume greater responsibility for maintaining order and security. This continued troop presence reflects a cautious approach to the transition, acknowledging that Iraqi forces may still require assistance and backup as they take on primary security duties.

Brigadier Gen. David Perkins characterized the handover as a milestone achievement, not just for Anbar but for Iraq as a whole. His comments placed the transfer within the broader context of the country's provincial security transitions, noting that Anbar has now become the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to revert to local control. Perhaps more notably, Anbar holds the distinction of being the first Sunni-dominated province to achieve this status, a symbolically important development given the sectarian dynamics that have shaped much of Iraq's conflict since the 2003 invasion. This achievement signals potential progress in extending stability to areas that have historically been centers of resistance and violence, offering a template that could potentially be replicated in other predominantly Sunni regions still under coalition security oversight.

# Coalition Forces Transfer Security Control of Anbar Province to Iraqi Authorities

In a significant milestone for the ongoing effort to stabilize Iraq, coalition forces officially handed over security control of Anbar province to Iraqi authorities in a formal ceremony marking one of the most dramatic turnarounds of the war. Once considered the deadliest region in Iraq and the primary stronghold of al-Qaeda's insurgency, Anbar province had for years been synonymous with fierce sectarian violence, roadside bombings, and intense combat operations that claimed the lives of hundreds of American troops.

The transfer of authority represents the culmination of a strategic shift that began with the "Anbar Awakening," a movement in which Sunni tribal leaders—disillusioned with al-Qaeda's brutal tactics and extremist ideology—turned against the insurgents and allied themselves with coalition forces. This grassroots rejection of al-Qaeda, combined with the broader U.S. troop surge strategy, helped transform the province from a war zone into a relative model of stability.

While security responsibilities now officially rest with Iraqi police and military forces, U.S. troops will continue to maintain a presence in the province, providing support, training, and backup to Iraqi units as they assume greater responsibility for maintaining order. Military officials emphasized that this arrangement reflects a change in mission rather than a complete withdrawal, with American forces shifting from a primary combat role to an advisory and supportive one.

President Bush characterized the handover as a major achievement in the broader campaign in Iraq, emphasizing its symbolic and strategic importance. Anbar now becomes the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to achieve local security control, but perhaps more significantly, it stands as the first Sunni-majority province to reach this milestone. Given that the Sunni community formed the backbone of the insurgency in the war's early years, this transfer carries particular weight as an indicator of reconciliation and progress.

The handover comes against the backdrop of a broader, sustained decline in violence throughout Iraq, with monthly casualty figures and attack rates falling significantly from their peak levels. Administration officials pointed to this trend as validation of the surge strategy and the broader counterinsurgency approach adopted in recent years, suggesting that similar transfers of authority could continue in remaining provinces as security conditions permit.

# The Ancient City of Baghdad: A Modern Perspective

Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, stands as one of the most historically significant cities in the Middle East. Founded in 762 CE, the city once served as the center of the Islamic Golden Age, renowned for its contributions to science, philosophy, mathematics, and literature during the Abbasid Caliphate.

In recent decades, Baghdad has frequently appeared in international news coverage, particularly through outlets like CNN, which has extensively reported on the city's transformation through periods of conflict, reconstruction, and resilience. From the Gulf War to the 2003 invasion and subsequent years of instability, CNN's coverage brought Baghdad's struggles and triumphs into homes around the world, shaping global perceptions of both the city and Iraq as a whole.

Today, Baghdad continues to work toward rebuilding its infrastructure and reclaiming its historical identity as a cultural and intellectual hub. Despite the challenges the city has faced, efforts to restore landmarks, revitalize the economy, and improve daily life for its residents continue. International media organizations, including CNN, still maintain a presence in the region, reporting on political developments, security situations, and the ongoing efforts toward stability in Iraq.

The story of Baghdad reflects the broader narrative of Iraq itself—a nation with deep historical roots navigating the complexities of the modern world while striving to reclaim its place as a center of culture and progress in the region.

# U.S. Military Hands Over Security Control of Anbar Province to Iraqi Forces

**RAMADI, Iraq** — In a ceremony marking a significant milestone in the Iraq War, American military commanders formally transferred security control of Anbar province to Iraqi forces on Monday, ending years of intense U.S. combat operations in what was once the deadliest region in the country for American troops.

The handover ceremony, held at a provincial government building in Ramadi, was attended by U.S. military officials, Iraqi government representatives, and tribal sheikhs who played a crucial role in turning the province from an insurgent stronghold into a relative success story for American counterinsurgency efforts.

"This is a proud day for the people of Anbar and for the Iraqi security forces who have worked so hard to reach this point," said the senior U.S. military commander overseeing the transition. "Anbar was once written off as a lost cause. Today, it stands as an example of what is possible when local leaders, coalition forces, and Iraqi security forces work together."

Anbar, Iraq's largest province by geography, was once considered the epicenter of the Sunni insurgency following the 2003 U.S.-led invasion. Cities like Fallujah and Ramadi saw some of the bloodiest fighting of the war, with American forces engaged in prolonged urban combat against al Qaeda in Iraq and other insurgent groups.

The turning point came with the emergence of the "Anbar Awakening," a movement in which Sunni tribal leaders, disillusioned with the brutal tactics of al Qaeda-linked militants, began cooperating with American forces starting in 2006. Thousands of local fighters joined U.S.-backed groups known as "Sons of Iraq," helping to drive out insurgents and stabilize the region.

Military officials say violence in the province has dropped dramatically in recent years, though they caution that challenges remain.

"We are not saying the fight is over," one U.S. officer said. "But Iraqi forces have shown they are capable of maintaining security here, and it's time for them to take the lead."

Iraqi officials welcomed the transfer as a step toward greater national sovereignty. "This is a moment of pride for all Iraqis," said a provincial council member. "Our forces are ready to protect our own people."

Under the agreement, U.S. troops will maintain a reduced presence in Anbar, available to support Iraqi forces if requested, but will no longer lead day-to-day security operations. The move is part of a broader strategy to gradually shift responsibility for security across Iraq to national forces ahead of an eventual drawdown of American troops.

Analysts note that the handover carries symbolic as well as strategic weight. Anbar's transformation—from a region where American commanders once questioned whether the war could be won, to one now held up as a model of cooperation—has been cited by U.S. officials as evidence of progress in Iraq.

Still, questions remain about the long-term stability of the province and the ability of Iraqi forces to prevent a resurgence of extremist elements. Sectarian tensions and political disputes between Sunni leaders and the Shiite-led central government in Baghdad continue to simmer beneath the surface.

For now, however, the mood in Ramadi was one of cautious optimism. Residents lined streets near the ceremony, some waving Iraqi flags, as local police and army units took up positions once patrolled by U.S. Marines and soldiers.

"We have paid a heavy price for our freedom," said one Ramadi resident. "We hope this is the beginning of a new chapter."

The transfer of Anbar follows similar handovers in other Iraqi provinces as part of the broader U.S. military strategy to return control to Iraqi authorities. Officials say more provinces are expected to follow suit in the coming months as part of the continued transition of security responsibilities across the country.

**Iraqi Forces Assume Security Control of Anbar Province**

*Ramadi, Iraq* — In a ceremony held in Ramadi, U.S. and Iraqi officials formally transferred security responsibility for Anbar province to Iraqi forces, marking a significant milestone in a region once considered the heart of the insurgency and among the most violent areas of the country.

Anbar, a vast western province bordering Syria and Jordan, was for years synonymous with fierce fighting, particularly in cities like Fallujah and Ramadi. The turnaround has been attributed largely to the "Anbar Awakening," a movement in which local Sunni tribal leaders turned against al-Qaeda-linked militants and allied with coalition forces.

It was once written off as lost, and now it is a symbol of what is possible when local leaders and citizens reject terror and reclaim their communities," Bush said in a statement issued from Washington. "This transfer reflects the courage of the Iraqi people and the professionalism of Iraqi security forces who are increasingly able to protect their own citizens."

A U.S. military spokesperson in Baghdad echoed that sentiment, emphasizing the practical significance of the transfer. "This is a province that not long ago was the deadliest in Iraq for coalition forces," the spokesperson said. The progress here has been remarkable, and it reflects months of hard work by Iraqi and coalition forces alike."

# Iraqi Forces Assume Security Control in Anbar Province

**BAGHDAD** — Iraqi security forces formally took over responsibility for maintaining order in Anbar province from U.S. troops in a ceremony held this week, marking a significant milestone in a region that just three years ago was considered the epicenter of the Sunni insurgency.

The handover, attended by senior Iraqi government officials and American military commanders, symbolizes the dramatic security transformation in the vast western province, once synonymous with al-Qaeda strongholds in cities like Fallujah and Ramadi.

## From Insurgency to Awakening

Anbar's turnaround is widely credited to the Awakening movement (Sahwa), a network of Sunni tribal fighters who broke with al-Qaeda in Iraq beginning in late 2006. Disillusioned by the group's brutal tactics and extremist ideology, tribal leaders formed armed councils that partnered with U.S. forces, helping drive militants from cities and towns across the province.

Tens of thousands of Awakening fighters were absorbed into checkpoint duty and local security roles, receiving salaries funded initially by the U.S. military. The model was later replicated in Sunni areas around Baghdad and Diyala province, contributing to the broader decline in nationwide violence.

Despite this success, the transition of Awakening fighters into the Iraqi state apparatus has been fraught with difficulty. Many tribal leaders and fighters remain deeply distrustful of the Shiite-led central government in Baghdad, which has been slow to integrate them into the national police and army as promised. Reports of delayed salary payments, arrests of Awakening leaders, and what critics describe as sidelining of Sunni figures from political power have fueled resentment.

## Political Tensions Persist

The security handover comes against a backdrop of unresolved Sunni political grievances. Many in Anbar's political and tribal establishment complain that Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki's government has failed to deliver on promises of reconciliation, reconstruction funding, and a genuine share of power in Baghdad.

Provincial council elections earlier this year produced significant shifts in Anbar's political landscape, with tribal-based parties and former Awakening-linked figures competing against established Sunni Islamist parties for influence. The results reflected broader fragmentation within the Sunni political community, as different factions vie to represent a population still wary of both al-Qaeda's legacy and what many view as marginalization by the central government.

Sunni leaders have repeatedly warned that without genuine political inclusion — including fair distribution of oil revenues, jobs, and government positions — the security gains achieved through the Awakening could prove fragile.

## Cautious Optimism

U.S. officials have pointed to the Anbar handover as evidence of progress toward the broader withdrawal of American forces from Iraq, in line with the security agreement governing the U.S. military presence. Iraqi officials, for their part, characterized the transfer as a source of national pride, signaling that provincial forces are now capable of maintaining security independently.

Still, analysts caution that the durability of Anbar's peace depends heavily on whether Baghdad can address the underlying political disputes that fueled the insurgency in the first place. The fate of the Awakening fighters — many of whom still await full integration into state security forces — remains a key test of the government's commitment to reconciliation.

"The guns have gone quiet, but the political battle is far from over," said one Western diplomat in Baghdad, speaking on condition of anonymity. "Anbar's security is only as strong as the political arrangements that underpin it."

---

*This article reflects a composite portrayal based on real historical dynamics in Anbar province circa 2008–2009 and does not describe a specific verified news event.*

# Iraq Marks 11th Provincial Security Handover as Anbar's Transformation Continues

**BAGHDAD** — Iraqi and coalition officials on Monday celebrated the transfer of security responsibility for another province to Iraqi forces, marking the 11th such handover since the process began—a milestone that underscores the country's gradual, province-by-province transition away from foreign military oversight.

The ceremony, attended by Iraqi government officials, provincial leaders, and representatives from the U.S.-led coalition, formally placed local security operations under the command of Iraqi police and army units, with coalition forces shifting into a supporting and advisory role.

## A Symbol of Change

While each handover carries significance, none has resonated as powerfully as the transfer that took place in Anbar province, once regarded as the epicenter of the insurgency and among the most dangerous regions in the country. Cities such as Fallujah and Ramadi became synonymous with prolonged, intense fighting in the years following the 2003 invasion, as insurgent networks and al-Qaeda-affiliated militants entrenched themselves among the province's Sunni tribal population.

For years, Anbar was considered virtually unwinnable by many military analysts. Coalition and Iraqi forces suffered heavy casualties in the province, and until recent years, few would have predicted that local forces would be positioned to assume full security control.

The turning point came with the emergence of the "Anbar Awakening," a movement in which Sunni tribal leaders—frustrated by the brutal tactics and extremist ideology of al-Qaeda in Iraq—turned against the insurgency and aligned with coalition and Iraqi government forces. This grassroots shift, combined with sustained military operations, gradually eroded the insurgency's grip on the province and paved the way for the restoration of local governance and security infrastructure.

## Officials Reflect on Progress

Speaking at the handover ceremony, Iraqi officials emphasized the symbolic weight of Anbar's transition.

"This is not just a transfer of authority—it is a testament to the resilience of the Anbari people and the sacrifices made by our security forces," one provincial official said. "A province once written off as lost has become a model for what cooperation between local communities and government forces can achieve."

Coalition representatives echoed this sentiment, noting that Anbar's progress reflects broader gains across Iraq, even as challenges with residual insurgent activity, sectarian tensions, and rebuilding efforts persist.

## The Road Ahead

With 11 provinces now under Iraqi security control, attention turns to the remaining provinces still awaiting handover. Officials have indicated that the pace of future transitions will depend on local security conditions, the readiness of Iraqi forces, and continued coordination with coalition partners.

Analysts caution that while the handovers represent important milestones, they do not signal the end of security challenges in Iraq. Sustained investment in training, equipment, and governance will remain critical as Iraqi forces assume greater responsibility for maintaining stability nationwide.

For residents of Anbar, however, the moment carries deep personal significance—a marker of how far the province has come from its darkest days, and a cautious step toward a more stable and self-governed future.
